chapter: Theater broadcasts, recordings and the road
title: Wartime bands, the Interstate show, Cobb's split-week acts and the Rampart Street Parade
summary: One long answer covers touring in the war, booking acts at Cobb's, Mr. Cobb's generosity and his opinion of the Rampart Street Parade.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: He insults me, gives me a can of metal polish. I said, well, I'll remember you, Mr. Miller, Mr. Arthur Miller. Just jealous, that's all. And everywhere I went, the bands were being depleted by the war, the best men were being tricked, drafted, and the leaders were taking jobs as bandmasters and all that stuff. It was a good thing they brought me along, because I was the one who would set the tempo, not the drummer, the strange drummer. I'd give them that, I'd play a waltz, I'd give them that, with the trumpet, not making three notes, it'd be so decisive that they were glad they had me. But I got the fluids, I lost ten pounds. I tried to stand up and play solos with the flu, but I showed up and I played, so I banged off every four weeks. When I got off the train, my wife didn't know me. I looked so bad. It was nice to know Adelaide News, and they loved me and all like that, they loved my player. And the show traveled as a unit, I got to know all the people on the show, they were all nice friends, you know. It was called the Interstate Center. I did a lot of things, like Mr. Cobb, when they started putting acts in, Mr. Cobb didn't know one act from the other, he didn't want to spend any money. And those were playing split weeks. You know what they call split weeks? Three days and then four days. Well I get the acts that were laying off. I had to build posters for $25 a piece and all they could eat. Carl's restaurant. Guy says, I spent more than $25 on the car. I said, you get it for nothing, sign the check, and $25. A hundred dollars they call. And he said, well we're going to do two songs. I said, yeah, you're going to do a dozen if they clap, because I know they're all hams, they're all one of them. They like you enough, they get on that floor and do it for 45 minutes. That's all they sure I needed. I had the tops. I got Mary Riley. I don't know whether I heard them, but she was another Bee Palmer. The Orient would bring in Bee Palmer, I'd have to go dig up another cool shower somewhere, so I'd dig them up out of loads or somewhere and get them for the split weeks. And Mr. Cobb loved me, and he should. Don't you think? Well he has. He has the highest 550 people a night. That's past history. I can prove it, but it's facts. And I get in my share. I was the only man he ever gave a Christmas present to. He gave me a hundred dollars and almost dropped in. And he had, another thing, he did give presents to the busboys. He employed only deaf-mutes as busboys. He was a kind man, he was a fine man. And I go to his farm, he had a beautiful farm out on old Gentile Road, you ever hear of it? Next to Robert Hall. They own all that Robert Hall. In fact, Mrs. Cobb died and left a couple of million dollars to her family. And I could have married one of her nieces. But she was fresh from Germany. Boy she was socks to hog her if you ever saw one. She had Germany written all over her face. She had nothing. But there was a wonderful family. I was sitting home on Broadway in St. Charles, a beautiful house. He had a ratzkeller with a piano, he loved music. And when I played the dealer session, I always had to play some German music. Because you got all the German captains and mates from the ships and all that coming in. And I bring them back to Germany a little bit. And one day he said to me, what are you doing with your money? I said, that's better. I'll send you a subdivision, he says, from golf ports. All built up for $15,000. I hold some. I said, why? He said, I don't want to be bothered. I said, if I owe this man $15,000, I got to be a lifetime job in this place. You know what I mean? But I didn't see any further than this. I didn't buy it. You're musicians. You're a musician. You're nothing else. Nothing else. You're a musician. You live and die. You're making arrangements and trying to improve the other guy who's better than you to start off with. You're trying to arrange them. Now my idea, I write this with the long record. It's the best, if you call it Dixieland, jazz still written, is South Ramport Street Parade. Every straight in that thing is a different idea. Did you notice that? And it was written by two fellas, Bob Haggard the bass player and Raymond Baduk the drummer who couldn't read a note as big as the Custom House. But maybe Raymond could whistle him.
